5 Axioms, definitions, and theorems

This chapter presents probability axiomatically, defines probabilistic independence, and proves the basic theorems of the probability calculus, which we then use to solve probabilistic problems.

5.1 Axioms

In addition to thinking of probability in terms of stochastic truth-tables, we can also present it axiomatically. The usual axioms for probability are the following:

Non-negativity: For every proposition φ,P⁡(φ)≥0\varphi, \Prb(\varphi) \geq 0φ,P(φ)≥0

Normality: For every tautology τ,P⁡(τ)=1\tau, \Prb(\tau) = 1τ,P(τ)=1

Additivity: For any two mutually exclusive propositions φ\varphiφ and ψ,P⁡(φ∨ψ)=P⁡(φ)+P⁡(ψ)\psi, \Prb(\varphi \lor \psi) = \Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\psi)ψ,P(φ∨ψ)=P(φ)+P(ψ)

With this axiomatic presentation of probability we can now prove theorems about it. Our first theorem is that the probability of a contradiction is always 0. We know from our work with stochastic truth-tables that this is true, for a contradiction is true in no row of a truth-table, and so the sum of the rows where it is true is 0! Compare that insight stochastic truth-tables give us to the following proof of the theorem:

Theorem 5.1. If φ\varphiφ is a contradiction, then P⁡(φ)=0\Prb(\varphi) = 0P(φ)=0.

Proof. Suppose φ\varphiφ is a contradiction. Let ψ\psiψ be an arbitrary tautology (for instance, (A∨¬A)(A \lor \neg A)(A∨¬A)). Given that φ\varphiφ is a contradiction and ψ\psiψ a tautology, φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ are mutually exclusive. So, by Additivity, P⁡(φ∨ψ)=P⁡(φ)+P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi \lor \psi) = \Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\psi)P(φ∨ψ)=P(φ)+P(ψ). Since ψ\psiψ is a tautology, so is (φ∨ψ)(\varphi \lor \psi)(φ∨ψ). Therefore, by Normality, P⁡(ψ)=P⁡(φ∨ψ)=1\Prb(\psi) = \Prb(\varphi \lor \psi) = 1P(ψ)=P(φ∨ψ)=1. Since P⁡(φ∨ψ)=P⁡(φ)+P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi \lor \psi) = \Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\psi)P(φ∨ψ)=P(φ)+P(ψ), by substitution 1=P⁡(φ)+11 = \Prb(\varphi) + 11=P(φ)+1. Subtracting 1 from both sides of that equation, P⁡(φ)=0\Prb(\varphi) = 0P(φ)=0. ◻

We also reintroduce our definition of conditional probability:

Conditional probability: For any two propositions φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ, provided that P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0, P⁡(φ∣ψ)=P⁡(φ∧ψ)P⁡(ψ).\Prb(\varphi \given \psi) = \frac{\Prb(\varphi \land \psi)}{\Prb(\psi)}.P(φ∣ψ)=P(ψ)P(φ∧ψ)​.

5.2 Independence

Suppose that we are betting on the outcome of the flips of a fair coin. In fact, the whole flipping procedure is fair: any given flip has a 0.5 probability of coming up heads and a 0.5 probability of coming up tails (we ignore other possibilities, such as that the coin lands on its side). Suppose that you have just seen 5 tails come up in a row. How do you think the next flip is going to come up?

If you think that the next flip is more likely to come up heads, the good news is that you are not alone–many people would think that. It is an intuitive answer: if 50% of the flips should come up heads, and so far there have only been tails, it seems as if heads are "due". The bad news is that this line of thinking is wrong. If you trust me that the flipping set-up is fair, then you know that the next flip is just as likely to come up heads as it is to come up tails. To think otherwise is to commit the "gambler’s fallacy".

What exactly is the fallacy? We said that any given flip has a 0.5 probability of coming up heads and a 0.5 probability of coming up tails. That means the probability of any flip is not affected by the flips that came before (if any). When the probability of one proposition is not affected by that of another, we say that these propositions are (probabilistically) independent. We can give a precise definition of independence by appealing to conditional probabilities:

Definition 5.2. Probabilistic independence: φ\varphiφ is probabilistically independent from ψ\psiψ iff P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0 and P⁡(φ∣ψ)=P⁡(φ)\Prb(\varphi \given \psi) = \Prb(\varphi)P(φ∣ψ)=P(φ).

The proviso that P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0 is there because, as we saw in Definition 4.2, P⁡(φ∣ψ)\Prb(\varphi \given \psi)P(φ∣ψ) is undefined when P⁡(ψ)=0\Prb(\psi) = 0P(ψ)=0.

Flippings of one fair coin are independent of each other, as are flippings of any number of coins. Another example of independence is sampling with replacement. Suppose we have an urn with 50 black balls and 50 white balls. Sampling with replacement consists of taking out one ball from the urn at random and then replacing it in the urn. Of course, the probability of the ball’s being black is 50%. If after replacing it you then draw another ball at random, the probability of that second ball’s being black is exactly the same: 50%. Indeed, even if you sample and replace 100 balls in a row and they are all black, the 101st draw is still 50% likely to be black. Of course, it may well happen that if you sample 100 black balls in a row you start to suspect that something fishy is going on: maybe a trick is being played on you, maybe you misheard the description of what is in the urn, or for some other reason the draws are not really independent of each other or random. But the point is that as long as you believe that the draws are independent of each other, past draws have no influence on future ones.

Coin flips are not just independent of each other, they are also unbiased: the probability of heads is the same as the probability of tails. That is what we mean when we say that a process is fair: the outcomes of the process have all the same probability and they are independent of each other:

Definition 5.3. Unbiased: a process is unbiased if and only if all the possible outcomes of the process have the same probability.

Definition 5.4. Fair: a process is fair iff it is unbiased and its outcomes are independent of each other.

5.3 Unconditional probability theorems

Let us now use the axioms and definitions to prove some more theorems. In each case, you can compare the discursive proof given here with your understanding of the theorem given by stochastic truth-tables.

Theorem 5.5. For any proposition φ\varphiφ, P⁡(φ)+P⁡(¬φ)=1\Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\neg \varphi) = 1P(φ)+P(¬φ)=1.

Proof. Because φ\varphiφ and ¬φ\neg \varphi¬φ are mutually exclusive, by Additivity, P⁡(φ∨¬φ)=P⁡(φ)+P⁡(¬φ)\Prb(\varphi \lor \neg \varphi) = \Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\neg \varphi)P(φ∨¬φ)=P(φ)+P(¬φ). Since (φ∨¬φ)(\varphi \lor \neg \varphi)(φ∨¬φ) is a tautology, P⁡(φ∨¬φ)=1\Prb(\varphi \lor \neg \varphi) = 1P(φ∨¬φ)=1. Since P⁡(φ∨¬φ)=P⁡(φ)+P⁡(¬φ)\Prb(\varphi \lor \neg \varphi) = \Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\neg \varphi)P(φ∨¬φ)=P(φ)+P(¬φ) and P⁡(φ∨¬φ)=1\Prb(\varphi \lor \neg \varphi) = 1P(φ∨¬φ)=1, by substitution, P⁡(φ)+P⁡(¬φ)=1\Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\neg \varphi) = 1P(φ)+P(¬φ)=1. ◻

Notice that you can use Theorem 5.5 to figure out the probability of any proposition φ\varphiφ if you know the probability of its negation ¬φ\neg \varphi¬φ, and vice versa.

Theorem 5.6. If two propositions φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ are tautologically equivalent, then P⁡(φ)=P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi) = \Prb(\psi)P(φ)=P(ψ).

Proof. Let φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ be tautologically equivalent. Since they are, (φ∨¬ψ)(\varphi \lor \neg \psi)(φ∨¬ψ) is a tautology and (φ∧¬ψ)(\varphi \land \neg \psi)(φ∧¬ψ) is a contradiction. So, φ\varphiφ and ¬ψ\neg \psi¬ψ are mutually exclusive. Therefore, by Additivity, P⁡(φ∨¬ψ)=P⁡(φ)+P⁡(¬ψ)\Prb(\varphi \lor \neg \psi) = \Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\neg \psi)P(φ∨¬ψ)=P(φ)+P(¬ψ). By Normality, since (φ∨¬ψ)(\varphi \lor \neg \psi)(φ∨¬ψ) is a tautology, P⁡(φ∨¬ψ)=1\Prb(\varphi \lor \neg \psi) = 1P(φ∨¬ψ)=1. Since P⁡(φ∨¬ψ)=1\Prb(\varphi \lor \neg \psi) = 1P(φ∨¬ψ)=1 and P⁡(φ∨¬ψ)=P⁡(φ)+P⁡(¬ψ)\Prb(\varphi \lor \neg \psi) = \Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\neg \psi)P(φ∨¬ψ)=P(φ)+P(¬ψ), by substitution P⁡(φ)+P⁡(¬ψ)=1\Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\neg\psi) = 1P(φ)+P(¬ψ)=1. By Theorem 5.5, P⁡(ψ)+P⁡(¬ψ)=1\Prb(\psi) + \Prb(\neg \psi) = 1P(ψ)+P(¬ψ)=1, which rearranges to P⁡(¬ψ)=1−P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\neg \psi) = 1 - \Prb(\psi)P(¬ψ)=1−P(ψ). Since P⁡(¬ψ)=1−P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\neg \psi) = 1 - \Prb(\psi)P(¬ψ)=1−P(ψ) and P⁡(φ)+P⁡(¬ψ)=1\Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\neg\psi) = 1P(φ)+P(¬ψ)=1, substitution yields P⁡(φ)+1−P⁡(ψ)=1\Prb(\varphi) + 1 - \Prb(\psi) = 1P(φ)+1−P(ψ)=1, which rearranges to P⁡(φ)=P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi) = \Prb(\psi)P(φ)=P(ψ). ◻

Two more basic results will be useful. First, no probability can exceed 1:

Theorem 5.7. For any proposition φ\varphiφ, 0≤P⁡(φ)≤10 \leq \Prb(\varphi) \leq 10≤P(φ)≤1.

Proof. By Non-negativity, P⁡(φ)≥0\Prb(\varphi) \geq 0P(φ)≥0. By Theorem 5.5, P⁡(φ)+P⁡(¬φ)=1\Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\neg \varphi) = 1P(φ)+P(¬φ)=1, so P⁡(φ)=1−P⁡(¬φ)\Prb(\varphi) = 1 - \Prb(\neg \varphi)P(φ)=1−P(¬φ). By Non-negativity, P⁡(¬φ)≥0\Prb(\neg \varphi) \geq 0P(¬φ)≥0, and so P⁡(φ)=1−P⁡(¬φ)≤1\Prb(\varphi) = 1 - \Prb(\neg \varphi) \leq 1P(φ)=1−P(¬φ)≤1. ◻

Second, a proposition cannot be more probable than a proposition that is true in every row where it is true:

Theorem 5.8. [Monotonicity] If ψ\psiψ is true in every row of the truth-table in which φ\varphiφ is true, then P⁡(φ)≤P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi) \leq \Prb(\psi)P(φ)≤P(ψ).

Proof. Suppose that ψ\psiψ is true in every row in which φ\varphiφ is true. Then φ\varphiφ is tautologically equivalent to (φ∧ψ)(\varphi \land \psi)(φ∧ψ), and so, by Theorem 5.6, P⁡(φ)=P⁡(φ∧ψ)\Prb(\varphi) = \Prb(\varphi \land \psi)P(φ)=P(φ∧ψ). As a matter of logic, ψ\psiψ is equivalent to (φ∧ψ)∨(¬φ∧ψ)(\varphi \land \psi) \lor (\neg \varphi \land \psi)(φ∧ψ)∨(¬φ∧ψ), and (φ∧ψ)(\varphi \land \psi)(φ∧ψ) and (¬φ∧ψ)(\neg \varphi \land \psi)(¬φ∧ψ) are mutually exclusive. So, by Theorem 5.6 and Additivity, P⁡(ψ)=P⁡(φ∧ψ)+P⁡(¬φ∧ψ)\Prb(\psi) = \Prb(\varphi \land \psi) + \Prb(\neg \varphi \land \psi)P(ψ)=P(φ∧ψ)+P(¬φ∧ψ). By Non-negativity, P⁡(¬φ∧ψ)≥0\Prb(\neg \varphi \land \psi) \geq 0P(¬φ∧ψ)≥0. Therefore P⁡(ψ)=P⁡(φ)+P⁡(¬φ∧ψ)≥P⁡(φ)\Prb(\psi) = \Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\neg \varphi \land \psi) \geq \Prb(\varphi)P(ψ)=P(φ)+P(¬φ∧ψ)≥P(φ). ◻

In particular, P⁡(φ∧ψ)≤P⁡(φ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) \leq \Prb(\varphi)P(φ∧ψ)≤P(φ) and P⁡(φ)≤P⁡(φ∨ψ)\Prb(\varphi) \leq \Prb(\varphi \lor \psi)P(φ)≤P(φ∨ψ), for any propositions φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ.

The Additivity axiom tells us how to find out the probability of a disjunction when the two disjuncts are mutually exclusive. But what if we have larger disjunctions, like (A∨B∨C)(A \lor B \lor C)(A∨B∨C)? And what if the disjuncts are not mutually exclusive? Let’s tackle these questions one at a time.

Suppose we have a set of pairwise mutually exclusive propositions {φ1,φ2,…φn}\{\varphi_{1}, \varphi_{2},\ldots \varphi_{n}\}{φ1​,φ2​,…φn​} Then:

Theorem 5.9. [extended additivity] If {φ1,φ2,…φn}\{\varphi_{1}, \varphi_{2},\ldots \varphi_{n}\}{φ1​,φ2​,…φn​} is a set of pairwise mutually exclusive propositions, then P⁡(φ1∨φ2∨…∨φn)=P⁡(φ1)+P⁡(φ2)+…+P⁡(φn)\Prb(\varphi_{1} \lor \varphi_{2} \lor \ldots \lor \varphi_{n}) = \Prb(\varphi_{1}) + \Prb(\varphi_{2}) + \ldots + \Prb(\varphi_{n})P(φ1​∨φ2​∨…∨φn​)=P(φ1​)+P(φ2​)+…+P(φn​).

Proof. Assume that {φ1,φ2,…φn}\{\varphi_{1}, \varphi_{2},\ldots \varphi_{n}\}{φ1​,φ2​,…φn​} is a set of pairwise mutually exclusive propositions. Then, by finite additivity, P⁡(φ1∨φ2)=P⁡(φ1)+P⁡(φ2)\Prb(\varphi_{1} \lor \varphi_{2}) = \Prb(\varphi_{1}) + \Prb(\varphi_{2})P(φ1​∨φ2​)=P(φ1​)+P(φ2​). As a matter of logic, since φ1\varphi_{1}φ1​ and φ2\varphi_{2}φ2​ are each mutually exclusive with φ3\varphi_{3}φ3​, then so too is (φ1∨φ2)(\varphi_{1} \lor \varphi_{2})(φ1​∨φ2​) mutually exclusive with φ3.\varphi_{3}.φ3​. Therefore, by another application of additivity, P⁡((φ1∨φ2)∨φ3)=P⁡(φ1∨φ2)+P⁡(φ3)\Prb((\varphi_{1} \lor \varphi_{2}) \lor \varphi_{3}) = \Prb(\varphi_{1} \lor \varphi_{2}) + \Prb(\varphi_{3})P((φ1​∨φ2​)∨φ3​)=P(φ1​∨φ2​)+P(φ3​). Since P⁡(φ1∨φ2)=P⁡(φ1)+P⁡(φ2)\Prb(\varphi_{1} \lor \varphi_{2}) = \Prb(\varphi_{1}) + \Prb(\varphi_{2})P(φ1​∨φ2​)=P(φ1​)+P(φ2​) and P⁡((φ1∨φ2)∨φ3)=P⁡(φ1∨φ2)+P⁡(φ3)\Prb((\varphi_{1} \lor \varphi_{2}) \lor \varphi_{3}) = \Prb(\varphi_{1} \lor \varphi_{2}) + \Prb(\varphi_{3})P((φ1​∨φ2​)∨φ3​)=P(φ1​∨φ2​)+P(φ3​), substitution yields P⁡((φ1∨φ2)∨φ3)=P⁡(φ1)+P⁡(φ2)+P⁡(φ3)\Prb((\varphi_{1} \lor \varphi_{2}) \lor \varphi_{3}) = \Prb(\varphi_{1}) + \Prb(\varphi_{2}) + \Prb(\varphi_{3})P((φ1​∨φ2​)∨φ3​)=P(φ1​)+P(φ2​)+P(φ3​). We can iterate this process for each φi\varphi_{i}φi​ to reach P⁡(φ1∨φ2∨…∨φn)=P⁡(φ1)+P⁡(φ2)+…+P⁡(φn)\Prb(\varphi_{1} \lor \varphi_{2} \lor \ldots \lor \varphi_{n}) = \Prb(\varphi_{1}) + \Prb(\varphi_{2}) + \ldots + \Prb(\varphi_{n})P(φ1​∨φ2​∨…∨φn​)=P(φ1​)+P(φ2​)+…+P(φn​). ◻

What Theorem 5.9 tells us is that additivity works not just for disjunctions of two mutually exclusive disjuncts, but for disjunctions of any finite number of mutually exclusive disjuncts.

But let us now go back to our other question about Additivity: what if the disjuncts are not mutually exclusive? How do we find out, for instance, the probability of a disjunction of atomic propositions (or molecular propositions which are not mutually exclusive)? It would help to visualize the space of possibilities. One way of visualizing it which we are familiar with is a truth-table, where each row represents a possible world:

We can also graphically represent the same space of possibilities using a Venn Diagram:

We can see both in the truth-table and the Venn diagram that if we calculate P⁡(A∨B)\Prb(A \lor B)P(A∨B) by adding up P⁡(A)\Prb(A)P(A) and P⁡(B)\Prb(B)P(B) we would be double-counting P⁡(A∧B)\Prb(A \land B)P(A∧B). Rather, what we want to do is to add the first row of the truth-table (equivalently, the intersection of AAA and BBB) just once, so that we end up with the probability of the region of the space of possibilities where either AAA or BBB are true:

So, if we know P⁡(φ)\Prb(\varphi)P(φ) and P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\psi)P(ψ), but we don’t know whether φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ are mutually exclusive or not, how do we determine P⁡(φ∨ψ)\Prb(\varphi \lor \psi)P(φ∨ψ)? Well, if just adding P⁡(φ)\Prb(\varphi)P(φ) and P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\psi)P(ψ) counts P⁡(φ∧ψ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi)P(φ∧ψ) twice, we can just subtract it once, and so we have the following generalization of Additivity: P⁡(φ∨ψ)=P⁡(φ)+P⁡(ψ)−P⁡(φ∧ψ)\Prb(\varphi \lor \psi) = \Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\psi) - \Prb(\varphi \land \psi)P(φ∨ψ)=P(φ)+P(ψ)−P(φ∧ψ), which for obvious reasons is sometimes called the inclusion-exclusion theorem:

Theorem 5.10. [Inclusion-exclusion theorem] For any two propositions φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ, P⁡(φ∨ψ)=P⁡(φ)+P⁡(ψ)−P⁡(φ∧ψ)\Prb(\varphi \lor \psi) = \Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\psi) - \Prb(\varphi \land \psi)P(φ∨ψ)=P(φ)+P(ψ)−P(φ∧ψ).

Proof. Left as an exercise for the reader. ◻

5.4 Conditional probability theorems

The inclusion-exclusion theorem determines P⁡(φ∨ψ)\Prb(\varphi \lor \psi)P(φ∨ψ) on the basis of three other quantities: P⁡(φ),P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi), \Prb(\psi)P(φ),P(ψ), and P⁡(φ∧ψ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi)P(φ∧ψ). But, assuming we are given P⁡(φ)\Prb(\varphi)P(φ) and P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\psi)P(ψ), how do we determine P⁡(φ∧ψ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi)P(φ∧ψ)? The next two theorems answer that question:

Theorem 5.11. For any two events φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ:

  1. if P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0, then P⁡(φ∧ψ)=P⁡(φ∣ψ)×P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) = \Prb(\varphi \given \psi) \times \Prb(\psi)P(φ∧ψ)=P(φ∣ψ)×P(ψ);

  2. if P⁡(ψ)=0\Prb(\psi) = 0P(ψ)=0, then P⁡(φ∧ψ)=0\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) = 0P(φ∧ψ)=0.

Proof. There are two possibilities—P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0 or P⁡(ψ)=0\Prb(\psi) = 0P(ψ)=0—that we will consider in turn.

  1. If P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0, then P⁡(φ∧ψ)=P⁡(φ∣ψ)×P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) = \Prb(\varphi \given \psi) \times \Prb(\psi)P(φ∧ψ)=P(φ∣ψ)×P(ψ).

    Proof. Suppose that P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0. By Definition 4.2, since P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0, P⁡(φ∣ψ)=P⁡(φ∧ψ)P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi \given \psi) = \frac{\Prb(\varphi \land \psi)}{\Prb(\psi)}P(φ∣ψ)=P(ψ)P(φ∧ψ)​, which rearranges to P⁡(φ∧ψ)=P⁡(φ∣ψ)×P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) = \Prb(\varphi \given \psi) \times \Prb(\psi)P(φ∧ψ)=P(φ∣ψ)×P(ψ). ◻

  2. If P⁡(ψ)=0\Prb(\psi) = 0P(ψ)=0, then P⁡(φ∧ψ)=0\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) = 0P(φ∧ψ)=0.

    Proof. Suppose that P⁡(ψ)=0\Prb(\psi) = 0P(ψ)=0. As a matter of logic, ψ\psiψ is equivalent to (φ∧ψ)∨(¬φ∧ψ)(\varphi \land \psi) \lor (\lnot \varphi \land \psi)(φ∧ψ)∨(¬φ∧ψ). By Theorem 5.6, since ψ\psiψ is equivalent to (φ∧ψ)∨(¬φ∧ψ)(\varphi \land \psi) \lor (\lnot \varphi \land \psi)(φ∧ψ)∨(¬φ∧ψ), P⁡(ψ)=P⁡((φ∧ψ)∨(¬φ∧ψ))\Prb(\psi) = \Prb((\varphi \land \psi) \lor (\lnot \varphi \land \psi))P(ψ)=P((φ∧ψ)∨(¬φ∧ψ)). (φ∧ψ)(\varphi \land \psi)(φ∧ψ) and (¬φ∧ψ)(\lnot \varphi \land \psi)(¬φ∧ψ) are mutually exclusive, and so by Additivity, since (φ∧ψ)(\varphi \land \psi)(φ∧ψ) and (¬φ∧ψ)(\lnot \varphi \land \psi)(¬φ∧ψ) are mutually exclusive, P⁡((φ∧ψ)∨(¬φ∧ψ))=P⁡(φ∧ψ)+P⁡(¬φ∧ψ)\Prb((\varphi \land \psi) \lor (\lnot \varphi \land \psi)) = \Prb(\varphi \land \psi) + \Prb(\lnot \varphi \land \psi)P((φ∧ψ)∨(¬φ∧ψ))=P(φ∧ψ)+P(¬φ∧ψ). Thus, since P⁡(ψ)=0\Prb(\psi) = 0P(ψ)=0 and P⁡(ψ)=P⁡((φ∧ψ)∨(¬φ∧ψ))\Prb(\psi) = \Prb((\varphi \land \psi) \lor (\lnot \varphi \land \psi))P(ψ)=P((φ∧ψ)∨(¬φ∧ψ)), P⁡(φ∧ψ)+P⁡(¬φ∧ψ)=0\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) + \Prb(\lnot \varphi \land \psi) = 0P(φ∧ψ)+P(¬φ∧ψ)=0. By Non-negativity, neither P⁡(φ∧ψ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi)P(φ∧ψ) nor P⁡(¬φ∧ψ)\Prb(\lnot \varphi \land \psi)P(¬φ∧ψ) can be negative. Thus, since P⁡(φ∧ψ)+P⁡(¬φ∧ψ)=0\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) + \Prb(\lnot \varphi \land \psi) = 0P(φ∧ψ)+P(¬φ∧ψ)=0, it must be that P⁡(φ∧ψ)=P⁡(¬φ∧ψ)=0\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) = \Prb(\lnot \varphi \land \psi) = 0P(φ∧ψ)=P(¬φ∧ψ)=0. ◻

Since one of P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0 or P⁡(ψ)=0\Prb(\psi) = 0P(ψ)=0 must be true, (a) and (b) together establish the theorem. (When P⁡(ψ)=0\Prb(\psi) = 0P(ψ)=0 the conditional probability P⁡(φ∣ψ)\Prb(\varphi \given \psi)P(φ∣ψ) is undefined, which is why the first claim of the theorem is restricted to the case P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0.) ◻

As a special case of Theorem 5.11, we can prove that when φ\varphiφ is independent of ψ,P⁡(φ∧ψ)=P⁡(φ)×P⁡(ψ)\psi, \Prb(\varphi \land \psi) = \Prb(\varphi) \times \Prb(\psi)ψ,P(φ∧ψ)=P(φ)×P(ψ):

Theorem 5.12. If an event φ\varphiφ is independent of an event ψ\psiψ, then P⁡(φ∧ψ)=P⁡(φ)×P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) = \Prb(\varphi) \times \Prb(\psi)P(φ∧ψ)=P(φ)×P(ψ).

Proof. Let φ\varphiφ be independent of ψ\psiψ. By Definition 5.2, since φ\varphiφ is independent of ψ\psiψ, P⁡(φ)=P⁡(φ∣ψ)\Prb(\varphi) = \Prb(\varphi \given \psi)P(φ)=P(φ∣ψ). By Definition 5.2, P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0, and so by Theorem 5.11(a), P⁡(φ∧ψ)=P⁡(φ∣ψ)×P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) = \Prb(\varphi \given \psi) \times \Prb(\psi)P(φ∧ψ)=P(φ∣ψ)×P(ψ). By substituting P⁡(φ)\Prb(\varphi)P(φ) in for P⁡(φ∣ψ)\Prb(\varphi \given \psi)P(φ∣ψ), we get P⁡(φ∧ψ)=P⁡(φ)×P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) = \Prb(\varphi) \times \Prb(\psi)P(φ∧ψ)=P(φ)×P(ψ). ◻

Going back to our discussion of the Gambler’s fallacy, Theorem 5.12 tells us that the probability of getting six tails in a row is exactly the same as the probability of getting five tails followed by heads, namely 0.56=1640.5^{6} = \frac{1}{64}0.56=641​. To see why, let TiT_{i}Ti​ be the proposition that the iiith flip comes up tails. When we say that the flips of a fair coin are independent of each other, we mean that each flip is independent not just of each earlier flip taken separately, but of any combination of the earlier flips. So the sixth flip is independent of T1∧…∧T5T_{1} \land \ldots \land T_{5}T1​∧…∧T5​, and by Theorem 5.12, P⁡(T1∧…∧T6)=P⁡(T1∧…∧T5)×P⁡(T6)\Prb(T_{1} \land \ldots \land T_{6}) = \Prb(T_{1} \land \ldots \land T_{5}) \times \Prb(T_{6})P(T1​∧…∧T6​)=P(T1​∧…∧T5​)×P(T6​). Applying the same reasoning to the earlier flips, P⁡(T1∧…∧T6)=0.56\Prb(T_{1} \land \ldots \land T_{6}) = 0.5^{6}P(T1​∧…∧T6​)=0.56. The same goes for five tails followed by heads. This is just what the Gambler’s fallacy overlooks: the conditional probability of heads on the sixth flip, given that the previous five were tails, is the same as the conditional probability of tails on the sixth flip, namely 0.5, because every flip is independent of the previous ones.

Ignoring cases where one of the propositions has probability 0 (which can give rise to strange independence relations), probabilistic independence is symmetric:

Theorem 5.13. For any two events φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ, if P⁡(φ)≠0\Prb(\varphi) \neq 0P(φ)=0 and P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0, then φ\varphiφ is independent of ψ\psiψ if and only if ψ\psiψ is independent of φ\varphiφ.

Proof. Let P⁡(φ)≠0\Prb(\varphi) \neq 0P(φ)=0 and P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0. We prove the biconditional—that φ\varphiφ is independent of ψ\psiψ if and only if ψ\psiψ is independent of φ\varphiφ—by proving the two conditionals that constitute it.

  1. φ\varphiφ is independent of ψ\psiψ only if ψ\psiψ is independent of φ\varphiφ.

    Proof. Suppose that φ\varphiφ is independent of ψ\psiψ. By Theorem 5.12, since φ\varphiφ is independent of ψ\psiψ, P⁡(φ∧ψ)=P⁡(φ)×P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) = \Prb(\varphi) \times \Prb(\psi)P(φ∧ψ)=P(φ)×P(ψ). Since P⁡(φ)≠0\Prb(\varphi) \neq 0P(φ)=0 and P⁡(φ∧ψ)=P⁡(φ)×P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) = \Prb(\varphi) \times \Prb(\psi)P(φ∧ψ)=P(φ)×P(ψ), P⁡(ψ)=P⁡(φ∧ψ)P⁡(φ)\Prb(\psi) = \frac{\Prb(\varphi \land \psi)}{\Prb(\varphi)}P(ψ)=P(φ)P(φ∧ψ)​. By Definition 4.2, since P⁡(φ)≠0\Prb(\varphi) \neq 0P(φ)=0, P⁡(ψ∣φ)=P⁡(ψ∧φ)P⁡(φ)\Prb(\psi \given \varphi) = \frac{\Prb(\psi \land \varphi)}{\Prb(\varphi)}P(ψ∣φ)=P(φ)P(ψ∧φ)​. By Theorem 5.6 and the logical equivalence of ψ∧φ\psi \land \varphiψ∧φ and φ∧ψ\varphi \land \psiφ∧ψ, P⁡(ψ∧φ)=P⁡(φ∧ψ)\Prb(\psi \land \varphi) = \Prb(\varphi \land \psi)P(ψ∧φ)=P(φ∧ψ). Since P⁡(ψ∧φ)=P⁡(φ∧ψ)\Prb(\psi \land \varphi) = \Prb(\varphi \land \psi)P(ψ∧φ)=P(φ∧ψ) and P⁡(ψ∣φ)=P⁡(ψ∧φ)P⁡(φ)\Prb(\psi \given \varphi) = \frac{\Prb(\psi \land \varphi)}{\Prb(\varphi)}P(ψ∣φ)=P(φ)P(ψ∧φ)​, P⁡(ψ∣φ)=P⁡(φ∧ψ)P⁡(φ)\Prb(\psi \given \varphi) = \frac{\Prb(\varphi \land \psi)}{\Prb(\varphi)}P(ψ∣φ)=P(φ)P(φ∧ψ)​. Since P⁡(ψ)=P⁡(φ∧ψ)P⁡(φ)\Prb(\psi) = \frac{\Prb(\varphi \land \psi)}{\Prb(\varphi)}P(ψ)=P(φ)P(φ∧ψ)​ and P⁡(ψ∣φ)=P⁡(φ∧ψ)P⁡(φ)\Prb(\psi \given \varphi) = \frac{\Prb(\varphi \land \psi)}{\Prb(\varphi)}P(ψ∣φ)=P(φ)P(φ∧ψ)​, P⁡(ψ)=P⁡(ψ∣φ)\Prb(\psi) = \Prb(\psi \given \varphi)P(ψ)=P(ψ∣φ). By Definition 5.2, since P⁡(φ)≠0\Prb(\varphi) \neq 0P(φ)=0 and P⁡(ψ)=P⁡(ψ∣φ)\Prb(\psi) = \Prb(\psi \given \varphi)P(ψ)=P(ψ∣φ), ψ\psiψ is independent of φ\varphiφ. ◻

  2. φ\varphiφ is independent of ψ\psiψ if ψ\psiψ is independent of φ\varphiφ.

    Proof. Exactly as the proof of (a) above, but with every instance of φ\varphiφ replaced with ψ\psiψ, and every instance of ψ\psiψ replaced with φ\varphiφ. ◻

By (a) and (b), we have it that φ\varphiφ is independent of ψ\psiψ if and only if ψ\psiψ is independent of φ\varphiφ. ◻

We say that φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ are independent of each other (or just independent) when each of them is independent of the other. By Theorem 5.13, for propositions with non-zero probability this is the same as either one of them being independent of the other.

If a proposition φ\varphiφ has probability 0, then it is independent of any proposition ψ\psiψ that has non-zero probability—see exercises below. But if P⁡(φ)=0\Prb(\varphi) = 0P(φ)=0, then the probability of any proposition conditional on φ\varphiφ is undefined—see Definition 4.2—and so, by the definition of independence, no proposition at all is independent of φ\varphiφ.

5.5 Solving problems

Armed with the axioms and theorems of the probability calculus, we can now solve a number of probabilistic problems. Let’s try a sample one:

Assume: P⁡(H)=12,P⁡(G)=15,P⁡(¬F)=35,P⁡(H∨G)=35,P⁡(H∣F)=12,\Prb(H) = \frac{1}{2}, \Prb(G) = \frac{1}{5}, \Prb(\neg F) = \frac{3}{5}, \Prb(H \lor G) = \frac{3}{5}, \Prb(H \given F) = \frac{1}{2},P(H)=21​,P(G)=51​,P(¬F)=53​,P(H∨G)=53​,P(H∣F)=21​, and FFF and GGG are independent of each other.

What is P⁡(H∧G)?\Prb(H \land G)?P(H∧G)?

Try it in the Probability Lab Follow the solution step by step in the lab.

The basic strategy for solving any problem like this is to:

  1. Check what your goal is and note what’s involved in it.

  2. Check what you already have and write down anything that involves the same elements as your goal.

  3. Write down any axioms, theorems, and definitions that pertain to the kinds of things you are looking for or already have.

  4. Check if you have everything written down that you need in order to solve for your goal.
    If you do, just solve for your goal and you’re done!
    If you don’t...

  5. Repeat from step 1 with what you’re missing as your new goal.

Let’s apply this procedure to our sample problem. Our goal is to find out P⁡(H∧G)\Prb(H \land G)P(H∧G), which involves H,GH, GH,G, and conjunction. The second step is to check what we already have, which in this case is a lot. What is particularly relevant to our goal are the following:

  • P⁡(H)=12\Prb(H) = \frac{1}{2}P(H)=21​

  • P⁡(G)=15\Prb(G) = \frac{1}{5}P(G)=51​

  • P⁡(H∨G)=35\Prb(H \lor G) = \frac{3}{5}P(H∨G)=53​

  • P⁡(H∣F)=12\Prb(H \given F) = \frac{1}{2}P(H∣F)=21​

  • FFF and GGG are independent.

The third step is to examine the axioms, theorems and definitions to find if anything there is relevant to our goal.1 Definition 4.2 concerns conjunction:

Conditional Probability: For any two propositions φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ, provided that P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0,

P⁡(φ∣ψ)=P⁡(φ∧ψ)P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi \given \psi) = \frac{\Prb(\varphi \land \psi)}{\Prb(\psi)}P(φ∣ψ)=P(ψ)P(φ∧ψ)​

φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ are metavariables ranging over propositions of PL. What we are interested in is the conjunction of HHH and GGG, so we should apply Definition 4.2 to those propositions:

Provided that P⁡(G)≠0,\Prb(G) \neq 0,P(G)=0,

P⁡(H∣G)=P⁡(H∧G)P⁡(G)\Prb(H \given G) = \frac{\Prb(H \land G)}{\Prb(G)}P(H∣G)=P(G)P(H∧G)​

We are also given that P⁡(G)=15\Prb(G) = \frac{1}{5}P(G)=51​, so that the proviso of Definition 4.2 is satisfied. In order to solve for our goal—P⁡(H∧G)\Prb(H \land G)P(H∧G)—we need to know the values of P⁡(H∣G)\Prb(H \given G)P(H∣G) and P⁡(G)\Prb(G)P(G). We know that P⁡(G)=15\Prb(G) = \frac{1}{5}P(G)=51​, but we don’t know P⁡(H∣G)\Prb(H \given G)P(H∣G). Maybe we’ll have to find P⁡(H∣G)\Prb(H \given G)P(H∣G) as an intermediate step in solving this problem, so let’s not completely abandon this line of reasoning, but we can set it aside for now to see if there is some easier way to do it.

Going back to our list of axioms and theorems that are relevant to our goal we find Theorem 5.10, according to which P⁡(φ∨ψ)=P⁡(φ)+P⁡(ψ)−P⁡(φ∧ψ)\Prb(\varphi \lor \psi) = \Prb(\varphi) + \Prb(\psi) - \Prb(\varphi \land \psi)P(φ∨ψ)=P(φ)+P(ψ)−P(φ∧ψ). Instantiating this theorem to GGG and HHH gives us:

P⁡(H∨G)=P⁡(H)+P⁡(G)−P⁡(H∧G)\Prb(H \lor G) = \Prb(H) + \Prb(G) - \Prb(H \land G)P(H∨G)=P(H)+P(G)−P(H∧G)

Does this help? It does, because we know that P⁡(H∨G)=35,P⁡(H)=12\Prb(H \lor G) = \frac{3}{5}, \Prb(H) = \frac{1}{2}P(H∨G)=53​,P(H)=21​, and P⁡(G)=15\Prb(G) = \frac{1}{5}P(G)=51​. Substituting in those values in the above formula gives us:

35=12+15−P⁡(H∧G)\frac{3}{5} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{5} - \Prb(H \land G)53​=21​+51​−P(H∧G)

Adding P⁡(H∧G)\Prb(H \land G)P(H∧G) and subtracting 35\frac{3}{5}53​ from both sides gives us our solution:

P⁡(H∧G)=12+15−35=12−25=510−410=110\Prb(H \land G) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{5} - \frac{3}{5} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{5} = \frac{5}{10}- \frac{4}{10} = \frac{1}{10}P(H∧G)=21​+51​−53​=21​−52​=105​−104​=101​

Exercises

  1. Suppose you are going to draw a card at random from a standard deck. For each pair of propositions, say whether they are independent or not.

    1. AAA = the card is red.
      BBB = the card is an ace.

    2. AAA = the card is red.
      BBB = the card is a diamond.

    3. AAA = the card is an ace.
      BBB = the card is a spade.

    4. AAA = the card is a Queen.
      BBB = the card is a face card.

    Show solution

    (a) independent; (b) not independent; (c) independent; (d) not independent.

  2. For each of the following examples, say whether it’s an instance of the Gambler’s fallacy

    1. You’re playing cards with your friends using a standard, randomly shuffled deck of 52 cards. You’re about half-way through the deck and no aces have been drawn yet. You conclude that an ace is due soon, and thus the probability the next card is an ace has gone up.

    2. You’re holding a six-sided die, which you know to be fair. You’re going to roll it 60 times. You figure about 10 of those rolls should be threes. But after 59 rolls, you’ve rolled a three only five times. You figure that the probability of a three on the last roll has gone up: it’s higher than just 16\frac{1}{6}61​.

    3. You know the lottery numbers in New Jersey are selected using a fair process. So it’s really unlikely that someone will win two weeks in a row. Your friend won last week, so you conclude their chances of winning this week too are even lower than usual.

    4. You’re visiting a new country where corruption is common, so you aren’t sure whether the lottery there is fair. You see on the news that the King’s cousin won the lottery two weeks in a row. You conclude that their chances of winning next week are higher than normal, because the lottery is rigged in their favor.

    Show solution

    (a) Not the fallacy: drawing without replacement, the probability that the next card is an ace is 4/264/264/26, not 4/524/524/52, so the earlier draws really are relevant. (b) The fallacy. (c) The fallacy (in its reverse form). (d) Not the fallacy.

  3. Prove Theorem 5.10.

    Show solution

    φ∨ψ≡(φ∧¬ψ)∨ψ\varphi\lor\psi\equiv(\varphi\land\lnot\psi)\lor\psiφ∨ψ≡(φ∧¬ψ)∨ψ, and the disjuncts are mutually exclusive, so P⁡(φ∨ψ)=P⁡(φ∧¬ψ)+P⁡(ψ)\Prb(\varphi\lor\psi)=\Prb(\varphi\land\lnot\psi)+\Prb(\psi)P(φ∨ψ)=P(φ∧¬ψ)+P(ψ). Also φ≡(φ∧ψ)∨(φ∧¬ψ)\varphi\equiv(\varphi\land\psi)\lor(\varphi\land\lnot\psi)φ≡(φ∧ψ)∨(φ∧¬ψ), again mutually exclusive, so P⁡(φ∧¬ψ)=P⁡(φ)−P⁡(φ∧ψ)\Prb(\varphi\land\lnot\psi)=\Prb(\varphi)-\Prb(\varphi\land\psi)P(φ∧¬ψ)=P(φ)−P(φ∧ψ). Substituting, P⁡(φ∨ψ)=P⁡(φ)+P⁡(ψ)−P⁡(φ∧ψ).\Prb(\varphi\lor\psi)=\Prb(\varphi)+\Prb(\psi)-\Prb(\varphi\land\psi).P(φ∨ψ)=P(φ)+P(ψ)−P(φ∧ψ).

  4. Prove that if φ\varphiφ has probability 0, then it is independent of any proposition ψ\psiψ with P⁡(ψ)≠0\Prb(\psi) \neq 0P(ψ)=0. (Hint: by Theorem 5.8, P⁡(φ∧ψ)≤P⁡(φ)\Prb(\varphi \land \psi) \leq \Prb(\varphi)P(φ∧ψ)≤P(φ).)

    Show solution

    By monotonicity, P⁡(φ∧ψ)≤P⁡(φ)=0\Prb(\varphi\land\psi)\le\Prb(\varphi)=0P(φ∧ψ)≤P(φ)=0, so P⁡(φ∧ψ)=0\Prb(\varphi\land\psi)=0P(φ∧ψ)=0. Hence P⁡(φ∣ψ)=0=P⁡(φ)\Prb(\varphi\given\psi)=0=\Prb(\varphi)P(φ∣ψ)=0=P(φ) whenever P⁡(ψ)>0\Prb(\psi)>0P(ψ)>0.
